title: About nlp-quora-randomforest
tagline: Two questions in, the probability they ask the same thing out: 22 engineered features plus bag-of-words, voted on by a Random Forest.

sections.title: The Problem
body: Quora gets many questions that ask the same thing in different words. "How do I lose weight fast?" and "What is the quickest way to lose weight?" should share one page of answers, not split them across two. The task: given two questions, estimate the probability that they are **duplicates**.

Text makes this hard in two opposite ways. **Paraphrases** mean the same thing with few shared words. **Near-misses** share almost every word but ask different things ("a job at Google" vs "an internship at Google"). A model that only counts shared words gets both wrong.

sections.title: Approach — Why a Random Forest on Engineered Features?
body: This is the recipe from lecture 8 of the End-to-End NLP course: turn each pair into numbers a human can read (how many words they share, how similar the strings look), add a bag-of-words for each question, and let a Random Forest learn how to combine them.

Every input to the model has a name, so the "Why" panel on the demo can show exactly what the model saw. Sentence embeddings or a fine-tuned transformer score higher on this dataset, but they need far more compute than a CPU-only NAS container has, and they are much harder to explain. They are planned for a later v2 demo.

bullets.label: Why a Random Forest
bullets.text: The features live on very different scales: character counts, ratios from 0 to 1, fuzzy scores from 0 to 100, word counts. Trees need no scaling, and they pick up interactions such as "many shared words **and** the same first word" without anyone writing them down.

bullets.label: Why 100 trees, min_samples_leaf = 2
bullets.text: Fully grown trees (leaf size 1) scored 0.6 points higher, but the forest was 4× larger (388 MB in memory vs 88 MB) and training peaked at 1.5 GB of RAM instead of 0.6 GB. Leaf size 5 was smaller still but lost 1.4 points. Leaf size 2 is the middle; saved and compressed it is {{training.model_size}}.

bullets.label: Why a shared 3000-word vocabulary
bullets.text: One CountVectorizer is fit on both questions together, then applied to each separately. Column *i* then means the same word on both sides, so the forest can compare them.

bullets.label: Why 100k training rows
bullets.text: The lecture trained on 3k. 100k rows (stratified from 364k) lifts accuracy by about 2 points and keeps warm-up near 5 minutes on the NAS. The full set would take several times longer for a small gain.

sections.title: From Raw Text to Numbers
body: Both questions run through the same fixed pipeline before training and before every prediction. The demo page shows each question after every step.
The cleaned pair then becomes one sparse row of **6,022 numbers**: the 22 engineered features, then 3,000 word counts for question 1 and 3,000 for question 2.

bullets.label: lowercase
bullets.text: "Python" and "python" count as the same word.

bullets.label: replace_symbols
bullets.text: `%`, `$`, `₹`, `€` and `@` become words ("percent", "dollar"…), so "50%" and "50 percent" match.

bullets.label: strip_math_tags
bullets.text: Quora wraps formulas in `[math]` tags; the tags carry no meaning.

bullets.label: shorten_numbers
bullets.text: 5000 → 5k, 2000000 → 2m, so different spellings of the same number match.

bullets.label: expand_contractions
bullets.text: "can't" → "can not", "what's" → "what is". Otherwise "can't" and "cannot" would never share a token.

bullets.label: strip_html · strip_punctuation · collapse_whitespace
bullets.text: Remove stray tags and punctuation, then tidy spaces.

sections.title: The 22 Engineered Features
body: Each feature answers a simple question about the pair. They come in four groups. Stopwords are NLTK's English list ("the", "how", "is"…); the small 0.0001 in each denominator keeps empty questions from dividing by zero.
How much the trained forest relied on each group (share of its total impurity decrease, summing to 100% with the two bag-of-words blocks):

bullets.label: Basic (7)
bullets.text: Character length and word count of each question, number of shared words, total words, and `word_share` = shared / total.

bullets.label: Token (8)
bullets.text: Shared **content words**, shared **stopwords**, and shared tokens overall, each divided by the shorter (`_min`) and longer (`_max`) question. Plus: is the first word the same? Is the last word the same?

bullets.label: Length (3)
bullets.text: Difference in word count, mean word count, and the longest common substring as a share of the shorter question.

bullets.label: Fuzzy (4)
bullets.text: Four `rapidfuzz` string-similarity scores from 0 to 100: plain ratio, partial ratio (best matching substring), token-sort ratio (word order ignored) and token-set ratio (duplicate words ignored).

sections.title: Probability and the Threshold
body: The model returns a **probability** that the pair is a duplicate, not a bare yes/no. The label depends on where you draw the line. The slider on the demo moves that line in your browser; the probability itself does not change.

Which way to move it depends on which mistake costs more. Calling two different questions duplicates (a **false duplicate**) would merge them and hide one asker's question under someone else's answers. Missing a real duplicate only leaves two pages open. So a site like Quora would rather raise the threshold: fewer merges, each more likely correct.
Measured on the {{split.test_samples}} test pairs:

bullets.text: precision {{threshold_sweep.t30.precision}}, recall {{threshold_sweep.t30.recall}}, flags {{threshold_sweep.t30.flagged_pct}}% of pairs

sections.title: Model Architecture
body: Two cleaned questions become one sparse row: 22 engineered features, then a 3,000-word count vector for each question from one shared vocabulary ({{training.vocabulary_size}} words). The row stays sparse the whole way: dense, 100k rows × 6,022 columns would need about 2.4 GB.
A Random Forest of 100 trees (min_samples_leaf = 2, 2 CPU cores) votes; the share of trees voting "duplicate" is the probability. Saved model: {{training.model_size}}.

sections.title: Dataset
body: **Quora Question Pairs**, released by Quora in 2017, taken from the GLUE benchmark's QQP task (`nyu-mll/glue` on Hugging Face, pinned to one revision so every retrain sees identical data). Each row is two questions and a human label: duplicate or not.

GLUE's own test split has no labels, so this demo trains on GLUE train (363,846 pairs, 36.9% duplicates) and tests on GLUE validation (40,430 pairs). Training uses a stratified 100k sample to fit the NAS memory and warm-up budget; testing uses every validation pair.

The labels are known to be noisy: Quora's reviewers did not always agree, so a perfect score is not possible. Quora released the data for non-commercial use only, so it is mounted into the container at runtime and never baked into the image.

sections.title: What This Model Can't Do
body: The model never reads for meaning. It measures overlap: shared words, similar strings, matching first and last words. That is enough for about 4 in 5 pairs, and it fails in predictable ways. Two of the three example buttons on the demo show it.

bullets.label: Paraphrases with different words
bullets.text: "How do I learn Python quickly?" vs "What is the fastest way to learn Python?" mean the same, but share few words besides "learn Python". The model scores it below 0.5: **Not duplicate**.

bullets.label: Near-misses with the same words
bullets.text: "How do I get a job at Google?" vs "How do I get an internship at Google?" share every word but one. The model scores it above 0.5: **Duplicate**. A job and an internship are different questions.

bullets.label: Word order
bullets.text: Bag-of-words and most features ignore order, so "Is a dog bigger than a cat?" and "Is a cat bigger than a dog?" look almost identical.

bullets.label: Negation
bullets.text: "not" is one extra word. "Is it good to eat eggs every day?" vs "Is it not good to eat eggs every day?" look like near-duplicates.

bullets.label: Unseen words
bullets.text: Words outside the 3,000-word vocabulary add nothing to the bag-of-words part; only the fuzzy and overlap features still see them. New product names and slang are mostly invisible.

bullets.label: Domain shift
bullets.text: It learned from 2017 Quora questions. Other text, such as support tickets, search queries or other languages, will score unpredictably.

sections.title: Performance
sections.problem_type: Binary text-pair classification · GLUE validation held out · threshold 0.5
body: Trained on a stratified 100k sample of GLUE train, scored on all {{split.test_samples}} GLUE validation pairs, which the model never saw. About 37% of test pairs are duplicates, so always predicting "Not duplicate" would already score about 63% accuracy. The lecture's version reached about 78% on 3k rows.

confusion_matrix.annotation: The top-right cell is the costly error: pairs that are not duplicates but were called "Duplicate", which would merge two different questions. Raising the threshold shrinks it, at the price of more missed duplicates in the bottom-left.

metrics_detail.name: Accuracy
metrics_detail.what: Share of test pairs labelled correctly at threshold 0.5.
metrics_detail.why_chosen: The number the lecture reports, so this demo can be compared with it directly.
metrics_detail.watch_out: With 63% of pairs non-duplicates, a model that never says "Duplicate" scores 63%. Read it next to precision and recall.

metrics_detail.name: Precision (duplicate)
metrics_detail.what: Of the pairs called "Duplicate", the share that really are.
metrics_detail.why_chosen: Tracks the costly error directly: every false duplicate lowers it.
metrics_detail.watch_out: Easy to raise by raising the threshold, at the cost of recall. See the threshold table above.

metrics_detail.name: Recall (duplicate)
metrics_detail.what: Of the real duplicates, the share the model found.
metrics_detail.why_chosen: Shows how many duplicates slip through and stay split across two pages.
metrics_detail.watch_out: Easy to raise by lowering the threshold, at the cost of precision.

metrics_detail.name: F1 (duplicate)
metrics_detail.what: Harmonic mean of precision and recall for the Duplicate class.
metrics_detail.why_chosen: One number that falls if either precision or recall falls.
metrics_detail.watch_out: Weights both errors equally, while here a false duplicate costs more.

metrics_detail.name: ROC-AUC
metrics_detail.what: Chance that a random duplicate pair gets a higher probability than a random non-duplicate pair.
metrics_detail.formula: area under the true-positive vs false-positive rate curve
metrics_detail.why_chosen: Judges the probabilities at every threshold at once, which is what the slider exposes.
metrics_detail.watch_out: Says nothing about whether 0.7 really means a 70% chance; that is calibration.

metrics_detail.name: Log loss
metrics_detail.what: How confident the model was when it was wrong (lower is better).
metrics_detail.why_chosen: The metric the original Kaggle competition used, and it rewards honest probabilities.
metrics_detail.watch_out: Random-forest probabilities are vote shares and are not calibrated, so this is higher than a model tuned for probabilities would get.
